titre: What Makes People Stay in an L2 Ecosystem?
texte: I’ve been thinking about what actually makes people stay in an L2 ecosystem after trying it for the first time. Low fees are obviously important, and incentives can bring in new users quickly. But I’m not sure either of those is enough to make people stay. For most users, the experience is much more practical. They move between wallets, DeFi apps, bridges and trading platforms depending on what they need. I work with BYDFi , so I see this crossover quite often. People usually don’t care much about putting everything into neat categories. They care about whether something is easy to understand, useful, and worth coming back to. That’s why I think retention is an interesting metric for ecosystems like Arbitrum. Getting 100,000 people to interact with an ecosystem once is great, but how many of them are still using it a few months later? And what actually makes them return? It could be lower transaction costs, better applications, liquidity, incentives, or simply a smoother overall user experience. I’d be interested to hear what people here think, especially those who have been using Arbitrum for a while. What makes you keep coming back to Arbitrum: the apps, fees, liquidity, UX, community, or something else?

titre: Exploring execution-time authorization for Superchain applications
texte: I’d like to get feedback from Optimism builders and the broader Superchain community on a potential infrastructure primitive for applications, payment flows, smart accounts and autonomous transaction systems. The problem Authorization can happen upstream of execution. Between that authorization decision and the point where an action is actually released, the executable payload can potentially become stale, altered, replayed, or otherwise no longer correspond to what was originally authorized. A2SPA addresses that specific boundary. It is an execution-time authorization layer that cryptographically binds the exact executable payload and relevant constraints — such as destination, amount, parameters, permissions and freshness/nonce — to a signed authorization artifact. Immediately before execution, the actual payload is verified against that authorization. If the action reaching execution is not the action that was authorized, verification fails. In simplified terms: Authorize → bind exact payload + constraints → sign → verify at execution → release only if it matches. A2SPA is not intended to replace wallets, account abstraction, policy engines, fraud controls, transaction simulation or existing security mechanisms. It provides a different assurance boundary: cryptographic evidence that the action authorized upstream is the same action that reaches execution. titre: Season 8 Growth Grants - TVL Impact Review
texte: gm all! Brichis here. I served on the Grants Council and on the Milestones and Metrics Council. Now the councils are dissolved and Optimism starts a new stage, so I did this analysis to close that chapter for me. I did it for fun, to learn new tools, and to show a different perspective: the view of a former councilor. I also want to keep the lessons from Season 8 before they are lost. I do not know what future programs will look like. But I hope these results help to define the next iterations of grant programs. I hope you enjoy it! If you have anything to add, feel free to DM me. TL;DR Nine Season 8 growth programs received 2.21M OP. In the targeted contracts, the ΔTVL was +$8.00M , or $3.62 per OP delivered . Six of the nine programs were positive. One grant, 40acres.finance, supplied 84% of the net total. 5 of the 8 grants with a Milestone 1 target reached it on at least one day in the incentive window. Of the seven grants with a full-program target, one reached it. Programs peak early and then lose the liquidity. The median program peaked on day 56, at 41% of its window. 1.27M OP is still in the claim contract. It belongs to grants that did not run a program, and the grantees did not claim it. Full report: brichis.xyz/reports/s8-growth-grants Code and data: github.com/brichis/s8-grant-impact-analysis Context Across Season 8, the Council approved 24 applications and used the full 6.29M OP budget. title: [Direct-To-AIP] Umbrella - Renew Allowances author: @TokenLogic created: 2026-09-25 Summary This proposal renews the Ethereum Collector’s allowances to the Umbrella RewardsController for the current reward period, ending on 2 December 2026. The proposed allowances are 500,000 aEthUSDT, 475,000 aEthUSDC and 160 aEthWETH, covering unclaimed rewards and the remaining emissions. Motivation Umbrella reward allowances are due for renewal. As stakers claim rewards, the RewardsController draws on the allowances granted by the Ethereum Collector. Governance periodically renews these allowances to support reward payments, most recently for aEthUSDT and aEthUSDC through AIP 507 . This renewal accounts for rewards accrued by current and former stakers, together with emissions scheduled through 2 December 2026. The Collector holds sufficient balances of the reward assets to fund these payments. Proposed Allowances The allowances are sized using unclaimed rewards as of 25 September 2026 and the maximum emissions for the rest of the period, rounded up. The calculation uses each market’s maxEmissionPerSecond to allow for deposits growing toward Target Liquidity. Current emissions are approximately 80% of that maximum for USDT and USDC, and 84% for WETH. titre: Security Council key exposure across three chains — draft for review
texte: Edit 21 Sep: report revised after the replies below, same link. §7 is rewritten since rotation doesn’t hold up as the mitigation, and the emergency count is fixed. Changes and credits are in §10. I’ve been looking at the Security Council path from a key-exposure angle and ended up with something I’d rather have checked before I publish it as final. Draft is up here: Reacher Report #002 If parts of it are wrong or already handled, I’d like to know before rather than after. Short version of what I found. The treasury contracts themselves have no private key, so a key-derivation adversary can’t touch them directly. The path runs through the council. Three things there: The twelve member addresses are the same across four multisigs on three chains — Ethereum emergency, Arbitrum One emergency, Arbitrum One proposer, Nova. That’s visible in the SecurityCouncilMemberSyncAction transactions in the L1 Timelock, nonce 18 from 6 August. One key per member, four seats. Public keys for at least nine of those seats are recoverable from chain data already. Safe signatures ride in execTransaction calldata, and the key comes back out of the signature. Three emergency actions have executed — KelpDAO recovery in April, the L2→L1 DoS patch in May, Stylus in October 2025 — nine signatures each. Against an ordinary attacker, 9/12 is nine different problems: different people, hardware, jurisdictions, habits, plus three org seats with their own internal controls. As a representative of Gateway.fm AS, node operator 35 in the Curated module, I would like to share the following post-mortem with the Lido DAO. Two unrelated incidents affected our validators in August 2026. Neither involved slashing and neither put stake at risk. Gateway.fm AS takes full responsibility for both. We have reimbursed the DAO 1.0054 ETH sent to the Execution Layer Rewards Vault on 2 September 2026 in transaction 0xaeca4781…b60014 . That figure is the DAO’s own calculation, which we accepted in full. We would like to thank the NOM workstream for producing it. Incident 1 — Validators without a signer, and invalid signatures during recovery 18–19 August 2026. Resolved. A batch of signing keys registered to our operator had no corresponding shares loaded in our remote signer. The gap had no symptom while those keys stayed undeposited. When the protocol deposited into that range, eight validators activated with no signer and could not attest, for between 7.5 and 13.1 hours each. While restoring the missing shares, a misconfiguration in our signing cluster caused signatures to be rejected by the network. This affected approximately 7,300 validators for 75 minutes. There was no slashing. An absent key produces no signature at all, and a malformed signature is rejected before inclusion. No double-signing occurred at any point.
